title: Red-shift & Big Bang
examples: What is the evidence that supports the Big Bang theory?
How do scientists know the universe expanded?
Can you explain redshift in simple terms?

explain.say: We can look at how light changes as it travels through space.
Distant galaxies show a pattern called redshift in their light.
This stretching of light means the source is moving away from us.
This shows that galaxies are moving apart from each other.
Another key piece of evidence is the cosmic microwave background radiation.

draw.text: CMB: Echo of the Big Bang

explain.say: This background glow matches predictions from the Big Bang model very well.

faq.q: What does redshift actually mean for light?
faq.a: It means the light waves have stretched out, making them appear redder than they should be. This stretching is evidence of movement away from us.
asks: What does the color shift tell us?

faq.q: Is everything moving away from everything else?
faq.a: Yes, the space itself is expanding, carrying the galaxies along with it. It is not that we are at the center of everything.
asks: Are we at the center of the universe?
Does everything move away from one point?

faq.q: What is the cosmic microwave background radiation?
faq.a: It is faint, uniform radiation that fills all of space. Scientists believe it is the leftover heat from when the universe cooled after the Big Bang.
asks: Where does the CMB come from?
Is the CMB proof of the Big Bang?

faq.q: How do we measure the redshift?
faq.a: Astronomers measure the spectral lines in the light from distant objects. If those lines are shifted toward the red end of the spectrum, it indicates redshift.
asks: Do we need special equipment to see it?

faq.q: Does redshift mean the object is moving through space?
faq.a: No, it means that the space between us and the object is expanding. The space itself is stretching the light waves.
asks: Is it like an expanding balloon?
Is it the object moving through space?

facts: Redshift is the stretching of light waves toward longer, redder wavelengths.
The observed redshift of distant galaxies suggests the universe is expanding.
The Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) is leftover heat from the early universe.
The CMB temperature is very close to 2.7 degrees above absolute zero.

quiz.say: If the light from a galaxy is shifted toward the blue end of the spectrum, what does that suggest?

options.show: The object is much farther away.
options.say: The object is much farther away.

options.show: The light source is burning hotter.
options.say: The light source is burning hotter.

options.show: The object is moving toward us.
options.say: The object is moving toward us.

quiz.why: Blue-shifting indicates that the waves are compressed, which happens when the source is moving closer to the observer.

wrong.0: Distance alone does not determine the color shift; motion is the key factor here.
wrong.1: While temperature affects light, the observed shift is due to the Doppler effect from motion.
wrong.2: Rotation causes different shifts, but the consistent shift across many galaxies points to overall expansion.

quiz.say: What is the primary evidence supporting the Big Bang theory?

options.show: The combination of redshift and the CMB.
options.say: The combination of redshift and the CMB.

quiz.why: Both the expanding redshift of galaxies and the uniform background radiation match the predictions of the Big Bang model.

wrong.1: While important, redshift alone is not enough; the CMB provides crucial confirmation.
wrong.2: The existence of galaxies is expected in any universe; we need evidence of its origin.
wrong.3: The speed of light is a constant, not direct evidence of the universe's beginning.

quiz.say: The CMB radiation is best described as:

options.show: A signal from an alien civilization.
options.say: A signal from an alien civilization.

quiz.why: It is a nearly uniform glow of microwave radiation filling all space, exactly as predicted by cooling models.

wrong.0: Starlight comes from specific, localized sources, not a uniform background glow.
wrong.1: While intriguing, its measured spectrum matches natural cosmological predictions, not artificial signals.
wrong.2: Lensing bends light from specific objects, it does not create a uniform background glow.
